extracted.intended_audience: psychology researchers and graduate students studying cognitive theories of humor and experimental humor appreciation
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conceptual/experimental guidance for analyzing how structural incongruity (nonsense vs incongruity-resolution), processing variables (comprehension, simultaneity, emotional/cognitive tolerance), personality, and context determine humor appreciation. Useful for designing, scoring, or interpreting empirical studies of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Incongruity is defined as 'the simultaneous presence of two or more habitually incompatible elements, where an element can be either an object or an event'" (Shultz, 1972, p.457). Also characterized as "the unexpected meaning of one element [that] changes the meaning of the whole" (Gestalt account, McGhee, 1979).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incongruity is the structural core of humor stimuli; it may be unexpected, impossible, or improbable. Examples: the setup that primes an expectation prematurely ("how many academics...?") and a punchline that reverses figure/ground. Incongruity by itself produces surprise/cognitive arousal but is not necessarily humorous — it is the starting structural element to be evaluated for resolution, simultaneity, and affective acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution (role in two-stage models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolution is the second stage in Shultz's and Suls' two-stage models: after detecting an incongruity the recipient undertakes a problem-solving search that reunites the punchline with the joke body via a 'cognitive rule', logical proposition, definition, or fact of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolution (incongruity-reconciliation) renders incoherent elements coherent without making them serious and is argued to be required for a humorous response in two-stage models. Operationally, resolution is achieved when retrieval of relevant information reconciles the incongruous parts. Without resolution, incongruity may lead to puzzlement or negative emotion instead of amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two structural types: Incongruity-Resolution (INC-RES) vs Nonsense (NON)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes INC-RES (two-stage, has an intended, meaningful resolution) from NON (one-stage, pure incongruity or nonsense that may be bizarre or lack resolution). Ruch (1992) reports INC-RES is overall preferred, but NON can be amusing for some.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat INC-RES and NON as distinct stimulus structures in design and measurement. Empirical findings reported here: incongruity-resolution was rated significantly funnier than nonsense; both funniness and aversiveness ratings tend to be higher for INC-RES than for NON. ANTICIPATE: NON may be more arousing and require higher tolerance for ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree/types of resolution (Rothbart & Pien taxonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rothbart & Pien (1977) differentiate incongruity types: impossible incongruity vs possible incongruity; and resolution: complete resolution (initial incongruity follows completely from resolution information) vs incomplete resolution (initial incongruity is only partially reconciled or remains bizarre).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these distinctions to classify stimuli: complete resolution → clear INC-RES; incomplete or absent resolution → NON or partially resolved items. The degree of resolution predicts subjective reactions (e.g., arousal, funniness) and may interact with individual tolerance measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehension (cognitive prerequisite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comprehension of the conflicting ideas in an incongruous stimulus must precede appreciation: 'comprehension... is required for a potentially humorous response' (Bariaud, 1989).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure participants possess requisite background knowledge to understand stimulus relationships (example: knowledge of academics/graduate students in the 'lightbulb' joke). Comprehension is necessary but not sufficient for amusement — must be combined with simultaneity and tolerance/context factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneity (structural binding requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simultaneity: 'the multiple and incongruous aspects of the joke or cartoon must form a structured whole, with the contrasting meanings bound together and viewed simultaneously' (Leventhal & Safer, 1977).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stimuli should present incongruous elements as a coherent gestalt (figure/ground reversal). Simultaneity enables the recipient to accept impossible relationships as a related unit; it is a cognitive pre-requisite but not sufficient for amusement alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional tolerance / Emotional complicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional tolerance (aka 'emotional complicity' or 'playful frame of mind') is the affective requirement that the recipient accept incongruity as non-malicious and adopt the intended humorous stance. Emotional reactions to incongruity can be negative emotion, puzzlement, or amusement (Morreall, 1989).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure or manipulate affective stance: signals that reduce perceived threat (social cues, fantasy assimilation) increase probability of amusement. Emotional tolerance is not required for comprehension but is required for processing the stimulus as humorous rather than threatening/confusing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual differences: Conservatism and Sensation Seeking as predictors
rubrics_metrics.description: Ruch (1992) operationalizes personality-based emotional tolerance by combining Conservatism (Wilson, 1973) and Sensation Seeking (Zuckerman, 1979) to predict relative appreciation for NON vs INC-RES: Conservatives (intolerance of ambiguity) prefer INC-RES; Sensation Seekers (tolerance for ambiguity, desire for novelty) more often enjoy NON.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include validated personality measures (Conservatism, Sensation Seeking) when predicting structural preferences. Expect interactions: structure preference can be stable across content and related to need for certainty vs novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive tolerance / Need for Cognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Cognitive tolerance denotes a dispositional willingness to expend cognitive effort (Need for Cognition; Cacioppo & Petty, 1982). Those high in Need for Cognition enjoy effortful thought and make more discriminating judgments; this may predict preference for more intellectually challenging structures (e.g., NON).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Need for Cognition scale as a predictor of structural preference and processing style. Hypotheses: Conservatives may have low NFC and prefer INC-RES; Sensation Seekers may have high NFC and prefer NON. Consider NFC as distinct from emotional tolerance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context as social variable (fantasy assimilation / social cues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Social context includes cues (wry smile, telltale signals) that indicate the incongruity is intended as humorous (fantasy assimilation) and that affective distance/suspended belief is appropriate (McGhee, 1979; Bariaud, 1989).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manipulate or record social context cues in studies (presence of laugh track, teller demeanor, audience). Social context primes emotional complicity and can shift responses from negative/puzzlement to amusement. Social context is necessary to interpret a stimulus as intended humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context as cognitive variable (seriality, salience, priming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cognitive context concerns the configuration/serial position of stimuli (seriality). Priming increases salience of content or structural features; sequence rules (Forabosco, 1991) suggest: jokes rated more highly if presented in close succession; better order is from less incongruous to more incongruous; and structural linkage between jokes determines preferable order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design multi-item presentations carefully: manipulate primes to enhance salience of a shared feature (top-down selective processing). Expect context effects: priming a theme lowers threshold for subsequent appreciation; serial position and similarity/diversity across items affect funniness. Use priming to isolate the role of content vs structure (and to test salience vs Freudian drive predictions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Processing-variable interaction (comprehension, simultaneity, tolerance, context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor appreciation arises from interactions among cognitive and affective processing variables: comprehension, simultaneity, emotional tolerance, cognitive tolerance, and context. Each is framed as necessary but not individually sufficient for amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing stimuli, ensure multiple conditions are considered: comprehension preceding appreciation; simultaneity binding elements; adequate emotional/cognitive tolerance; and appropriate social/cognitive context. Empirical designs should test interactions (e.g., personality × context × structure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome dimensions: funniness and aversiveness (and arousal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjective responses to humor stimuli include funniness and aversiveness; incongruity-resolution often yields higher funniness and aversiveness ratings than nonsense. NON may be more arousing and requires higher tolerance for ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect multiple outcome measures (funniness, aversiveness, arousal) rather than a single humor score. Interpret higher aversiveness alongside funniness as informative about emotional tolerance and bittersweet or aggressive humor. Expect structure-specific patterns (INC-RES > NON on funniness and aversiveness in these studies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental/manipulation guidance (priming, serial presentation, structural salience)
rubrics_metrics.description: To test context effects or structure preferences, manipulate salience (prime a feature), serial presentation (order and proximity), and emotional/cognitive conditions. Experiments 1 and 2 evaluated emotional tolerance, structural salience and context effects via prime and switch manipulations; prime of INC-RES in NON context can decrease appreciation for NON.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When operationalizing hypotheses: use priming to increase salience of a shared characteristic; vary seriality (close succession, order less→more incongruous); measure personality moderators (Conservatism, Sensation Seeking, Need for Cognition); and record multiple dependent variables (funniness, aversiveness). Beware context-induced suppression/enhancement effects (e.g., presenting INC-RES in a NON series can decrease appreciation for NON).
